assets.title: The handbook question that comes back every Monday
assets.content:
Subject: The handbook question that comes back every Monday
Preview text: The answer is already written down. orqAgent puts an agent over your documents and answers it in the channel.

Your handbook, answering questions in Slack

Hi there,

The same handbook questions come back to Slack every week. The answers are written down already — somebody still has to go and find them.

The usual route is keyword guesses and half-remembered page titles. Past a couple of hundred pages that stops landing, and every new hire starts over.

orqAgent is a no-code platform for building AI agents, and it is now available. You can put one agent over your own handbook documents and have it answer in the channel where the questions already arrive.

Upload PDFs, docs or plain text — the agent retrieves the most relevant context for every query, with no vector DB to manage. Slack connects by OAuth install, and the bot replies to mentions and channel messages.

If nobody at your company owns internal tooling, that is usually what stops a build like this. There is no backend of yours to host and no retrieval layer to maintain.

$0 to start — 1,500 free credits, no card required.

Point it at one set of policy documents and one channel. Whether the retrieval lands on the way your team words things is a question only your own handbook answers.

Create your first agent →

— the orqAgent team

P.S. Agent setup runs from the console — under two minutes to a first agent.

The email's central premise — that low-code stacks get a bot answering but aren't built for reliable production, and that self-hosting means managing a vector store — matches a documented problem context, not just an email-only claim. Where it stretches: it presumes the reader has already tried or is about to try a low-code/DIY build ('whoever built it has moved on', 'it leaves you running a vector store'), which is an anticipated failure mode from the sourced material, not something the profile establishes this specific person has lived through. That's a plausible-fit premise, not a confirmed one.

reader_verdicts.problem_now: The repeated-Slack-question problem is documented as a live, ongoing pattern for this role (profile constraint), so it's a real background irritant, not a one-off. But there's no established urgency or deadline — 'considering building' is not 'this is on fire this week.' The email invents a March ownership crisis as a hypothetical, not a fact about this reader's timeline.
reader_verdicts.stopped_at: By the account of the people who build them, it is not made for reliable production use — and it leaves you running a vector store so a bot can answer from a PDF.
reader_verdicts.biggest_doubt: It doesn't say what happens when the handbook is wrong, ambiguous, or the bot is confidently incorrect in front of the whole team — no mention of accuracy, citations, permissions/access control per Slack channel, or how it handles multiple documents/sources like Issue Trackers, which is explicitly part of what I was asked to consider. One agent, one doc, one channel is a toy test, not something I can evaluate against 'access to Handbook, Docs and Issue Trackers.'

fixes: Meanwhile the same policy questions keep coming back in Slack, and the answers sit in documentation people search by guessing at page titles.

Preview text: Nobody, if you configure one instead. orqAgent is hosted, installs by OAuth, and logs every answer.

orqAgent: configure the handbook bot, don't build it

Hi there,

The question is not whether you can build a Slack answer-bot over the handbook. It is who owns it in March, when whoever built it has moved on.

Meanwhile the same policy questions keep coming back in Slack, and the answers sit in documentation people search by guessing at page titles.

A low-code stack gets a bot answering fast. By the account of the people who build them, it is not made for reliable production use — and it leaves you running a vector store so a bot can answer from a PDF.

orqAgent is available today — a hosted place to configure one agent over your own handbook documents. Slack is an OAuth install, so the bot replies to mentions and channel messages.

You upload the PDFs, docs or plain text. The agent retrieves the most relevant context for every query automatically — no vector DB to manage.
